chapters.name: Chapter 1: How chatbots work, and your first bot

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What a chatbot is, and two ways to build one
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain the difference between a keyword chatbot and an AI chatbot.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of chatbots, you will explain how a keyword chatbot and an AI chatbot work, with a strength and a limit of each, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
A chatbot is a program you talk to by typing or speaking. You see them on websites ("How can I help?"), in games and in apps.
There are two main kinds. A keyword chatbot follows rules a person wrote: if the message contains "time", answer with the meeting time. It is simple and predictable, but it only knows what you taught it. An AI chatbot uses a large language model, which learned from huge amounts of text. It can answer almost anything in natural words, but it can also be wrong or make things up.
In this course you will build both for a real use, like answering new members' questions for your club, so you can see the strengths and limits of each.
Words to know:
- Chatbot: a program you talk to by typing or speaking.
- Keyword: a word the bot looks for to decide how to answer.
- Large language model: the kind of AI behind assistants like ChatGPT; it learned patterns from huge amounts of text.
Try it now: Pick a club, team or group you belong to. Write down five questions new members always ask, like when you meet, where, and how to join.
You can now explain how keyword chatbots and AI chatbots differ, and choose a real use for a bot.

check.q: What is a limit of a keyword chatbot?
options: It only knows what you taught it
It needs a large language model
check.why: A keyword bot follows rules a person wrote, so it only knows what it was taught.

check.q: You need a bot that always gives the exact same, checked meeting time. Which kind is safer?
options: An AI chatbot with no instructions
A keyword chatbot with the checked answer
check.why: Keyword bots are simple and predictable; AI bots can be wrong or make things up.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Planning your bot's job
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a simple plan: who the bot helps, what it answers and what it should never do.
This lesson builds toward: For a real club, team or group, you will write a bot plan with who it helps, five or more checked answers, a fallback answer and what it must never do, with every answer checked with the club advisor.
Good bots have a small, clear job. Write a bot plan with four parts: who it helps (for example, new members of the chess club), the questions it answers, the answers (checked with your advisor), and what it should say when it does not know.
Also decide what the bot must never do: never ask for passwords, phone numbers or home addresses, never pretend to be a real person, and never give advice about health, money or law. When in doubt, it sends people to a real adult, such as the club advisor.
An AI assistant can help you brainstorm more questions: "New members of a high school chess club might ask what? List 10." Then check the answers yourself.
Step by step:
- Write who the bot helps.
- List 5 to 10 questions it will answer.
- Write a short, checked answer for each.
- Write the "I don't know" answer that sends people to a real adult.
- List what the bot must never do.
Words to know:
- Bot plan: a short description of what a bot does and does not do.
- Fallback answer: what a bot says when it does not know.
Try it now: Write your bot plan: who it helps, your five questions with checked answers, your fallback answer, and three things it must never do. Ask an AI assistant for five more questions you might have missed.
You can now plan a chatbot's job, answers, fallback and safety rules.

check.q: What makes a good job for a bot?
options: A small, clear job, like answering new members' questions
Answering every question in the world
Pretending to be the club president
check.why: Good bots have a small, clear job.

check.q: AI suggests an answer about club dues for your bot plan. What do you do?
options: Leave dues out of the plan forever
Check it with the club advisor before adding it
check.why: Bot answers must be checked with the advisor, not taken from AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building a keyword chatbot in Python
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build and run a keyword chatbot in Google Colab.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Colab, you will build a Python keyword chatbot with a loop, keyword answers, a fallback and a goodbye, so it runs and answers at least five questions.
Open Google Colab at colab.research.google.com, sign in with an account you are allowed to use, and start a new notebook. The bot uses a loop that keeps asking for messages, and if statements that look for keywords.
Here is the pattern, line by line: while True: starts a loop that repeats. Inside it, msg = input("You: ").lower() reads the message in lower case. if "bye" in msg: print("Bot: See you!") then break stops the loop. elif "time" in msg: print("Bot: We meet Tuesdays at 3:30.") answers one question. else: print("Bot: I don't know. Please ask the club advisor.") is the fallback. Indent the lines inside the loop and inside each if.
Add one elif for each question in your plan. If you get an error, read the last line and the line number, check for a missing colon, quote or indent, and if you are stuck, paste the code and error into an AI assistant and ask it to explain.
Step by step:
- Open a new Colab notebook.
- Type while True: and indent the next lines.
- Read the message: msg = input("You: ").lower()
- Add if "bye" in msg: with a goodbye print and break.
- Add one elif per question, and an else fallback. Run it and chat with your bot.
Words to know:
- Loop: code that repeats; while True repeats until break.
- elif: short for else if: check another condition.
- break: stops a loop.
- .lower(): changes text to lower case so "TIME" and "time" match.
Try it now: Build your keyword bot in Colab with a goodbye, at least three answers from your plan, and a fallback. Chat with it and try one question it should not know.
You can now build and run a keyword chatbot in Python with answers, a fallback and a way to stop.

check.q: In the Python bot, what does the else line do?
options: Gives the fallback answer when no keyword matches
check.why: else catches anything the other checks did not match.

check.q: Your bot answers "time" but not "TIME". What do you add?
check.why: .lower() turns the message into lower case so both spellings match.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI helper bots, testing and safety

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing instructions for an AI helper bot
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write an instruction card that makes a free AI assistant act as your club's helper.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will write an instruction card with the role, checked facts, tone and limits that makes the assistant act as a club helper, so it sends unknown questions to the advisor and asks for no personal information.
You can turn a general AI assistant into a helper for one job by starting a chat with clear instructions. Some tools also let you save instructions as a custom bot; menus and age rules vary, so check your tool. Pasting instructions at the start of a new chat works in most assistants.
A good instruction card has: the bot's role ("You are the helper for the Lincoln High chess club"), the facts it may use (your checked answers), its tone (friendly, short answers), and its limits ("If you do not know, say: please ask Ms. Rivera, the club advisor. Never ask for personal information.").
Tell it to use only the facts you gave it. This lowers the chance it makes up meeting times or rules.
Step by step:
- Write the role: who the bot is and who it helps.
- Paste your checked facts and answers.
- Set the tone: friendly, short answers.
- Add limits: use only these facts; send unknowns to the advisor; never ask for personal information.
- Start a new chat, paste the card, then ask a test question.
Words to know:
- Instruction card: the written rules you give an AI assistant at the start of a chat.
- Role: who the bot should act as.
- Tone: how the bot sounds: friendly, formal, short.
Try it now: Write an instruction card for your club helper bot. Start a new chat in a free AI assistant, paste it, and ask three questions from your plan and one it should not know.
You can now write clear instructions that turn a free AI assistant into a focused, limited helper bot.

check.q: What does the "role" line on an instruction card do?
options: Tells the AI who it is and who it helps
check.why: The role line, like "You are the helper for the chess club", sets the bot's job.

check.q: Your AI helper answers questions about homework too. What do you add to the card?
options: A rule to use only the club facts and send other questions to the advisor
check.why: Limits keep the helper in its lane and lower the chance it makes things up.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Testing and improving your bots
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Test both bots with real questions and fix what fails.
This lesson builds toward: Given 10 realistic test questions, you will test both bots, mark each answer right, wrong or made up, and fix what fails, making at least one fix to each bot and testing again.
Testing means trying your bot the way real people would. Write 10 test questions: the five from your plan, a few asked in different words ("when do y'all meet?"), one with a typo, and one it should not answer.
Ask both bots each question and mark each answer right, wrong or made up. The keyword bot may miss questions asked in different words; fix that by adding more keywords. The AI helper may sound right but invent details; fix that by tightening its instructions.
Ask a friend or club member to try your bot too. People always ask things you did not expect.
Step by step:
- Write 10 test questions, including different wording and a typo.
- Ask both bots each question.
- Mark each answer right, wrong or made up.
- Keyword bot: add keywords. AI helper: tighten instructions.
- Have someone else test it.
Words to know:
- Testing: trying a program on purpose to find what does not work.
- Test case: one question or input you use to test a program.
Try it now: Run your 10 test questions on both bots, mark each answer, and make one fix to each bot. Test again to see if the fixes worked.
You can now test chatbots with real questions, find what fails and improve them.

check.q: Which belongs in a good set of test questions?
options: Only questions copied word for word from your plan
The same question asked in different words
check.why: Real people ask in different words and make typos, so tests should too.

check.q: The AI helper gave a confident but made-up meeting room. How do you mark it?
options: Made up, then tighten its instructions
check.why: Mark invented details as made up and fix the instructions.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making your bot safe and honest
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Add safety and honesty rules, then finish your club chatbot.
This lesson builds toward: Before you share your bot, you will add a greeting that says it is a bot, privacy and safety limits, and get your advisor's OK, with serious or unknown questions sent to a trusted adult.
A bot should say it is a bot. People deserve to know they are not talking to a real person. Start with a greeting like "Hi, I am the chess club bot. I answer basic questions. For anything else, ask Ms. Rivera."
It should protect privacy: never ask for or store passwords, phone numbers, addresses or school ID numbers. It should stay in its lane: no health, money, legal or personal advice, and it should point to a trusted adult for anything serious.
Before sharing a bot with your club, get your advisor's OK, follow your school's rules about AI and technology, and keep the answers up to date when meeting times change.
Step by step:
- Add a greeting that says it is a bot and what it does.
- Check it never asks for private information.
- Make it send serious or unknown questions to a trusted adult.
- Get your advisor's OK before sharing it.
- Update the answers when facts change.
Words to know:
- Transparency: being open and honest, such as saying a bot is a bot.
- Privacy: keeping personal information safe.
Try it now: Final task: finish your Python keyword bot (five answers, fallback, bye) and your AI helper instruction card. Add a greeting that says it is a bot, test both with 10 questions, write what each got right and wrong, and make one improvement to each.
You can now build, test and share a simple chatbot that is useful, safe and honest about being a bot.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Keyword bot works The bot does not run, or has fewer than five answers. Runs in Colab, greets the user, answers at least five questions, has a fallback and stops at bye. Also matches questions asked in different words with extra keywords. AI helper card The card is missing the role, facts or limits. Role, checked facts, tone and limits, and it sends unknown questions to the advisor. The helper stayed in its lane on a tricky test question. Checked answers Answers are unchecked or taken from AI. Every answer in both bots is checked with the club advisor. Includes a plan for updating answers when facts change. Testing and fixes Fewer than 10 tests, or no fixes. 10 tests on both bots, each marked right, wrong or made up, and one fix to each bot. Retested after the fixes and someone else also tested the bots. Safe and honest The bot does not say it is a bot, or asks for private information. The greeting says it is a bot, it asks for no private information, and serious questions go to a trusted adult. The advisor has approved it for sharing. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which of these should your bot never ask for?
options: Whether they want the meeting time
If they want to say bye
check.why: Bots should never ask for or store passwords, phone numbers, addresses or ID numbers.

check.q: Your bot is ready. What do you do before sharing it with the club?
options: Get the advisor's OK and follow school rules
Let it ask for phone numbers to follow up
check.why: Get your advisor's OK and follow school rules before sharing.
